cards.front: The inner ear has two parts that share the hair cell. Name them and what each senses.
cards.back: The cochlea, a coiled tube, analyses sound. The vestibular organs (three semicircular canals and two otolith organs) sense head motion and gravity.
cards.quote: The vestibular organs, three semicircular canals and two otolith organs, sense head motion and gravity.

cards.front: What single thing does a hair cell report, and what makes pitch, sound direction and head motion come out differently?
cards.back: Which way, and how far, its bundle is pushed. The differences come mainly from the mechanics in front of the cell (what pushes which bundle) and the circuits behind it (where, when, which side).
cards.quote: A hair cell reports which way, and how far, its bundle is pushed.

cards.front: In a hair bundle, what are tip links, and which two proteins form them?
cards.back: Fine links from the tip of each shorter stereocilium to the side of its taller neighbour, made of cadherin 23 and protocadherin 15.
cards.quote: Fine tip links run from the tip of each shorter stereocilium to the side of its taller neighbour.
cards.section: The hair bundle: force to current

cards.front: Why does it matter that some hair-cell transduction channels are already open when the bundle is at rest?
cards.back: The resting current lets one cell signal in two directions: a push toward the tallest stereocilia opens more channels (depolarizing), a push the other way closes the open ones (hyperpolarizing).
cards.quote: That resting current is what lets one cell signal in two directions.
cards.section: At rest, then pushed both ways

cards.front: A hair bundle is pushed away from its tallest stereocilia. What happens to the tip links, the channels and the membrane voltage?
cards.back: The tip links slacken, channels that were open at rest close, less current flows in, and the cell hyperpolarizes.
cards.quote: The links slacken and the channels that were open at rest close.
cards.section: At rest, then pushed both ways

cards.front: In a hair cell, 20% of transduction channels are open at rest. At a fixed voltage, how many times more room does the transduction conductance have to rise than to fall?
cards.back: About 4 times. It can rise by 80% of its maximum (to all open) but fall by only 20% (to all closed): 80 / 20 = 4.
cards.why: Conductance is bounded between all channels closed and all open, so a low resting fraction leaves most room on the opening side.
cards.quote: If 10% are open, conductance can rise by 90% of its maximum but fall by only 10%
cards.section: At rest, then pushed both ways

cards.front: In bullfrog saccular hair cells in vitro, single bundles were moved by known distances with a fine probe while voltage was recorded inside the cell. What did the recordings show?
cards.back: Deflection toward the kinocilium (tall side) depolarized; the other way hyperpolarized. The voltage was graded with distance, up to about 15 mV, and lopsided like the channel-opening curve.
cards.why: Those numbers belong to the frog preparation, not the human cochlea.
cards.quote: Deflection toward the kinocilium, the tall side, depolarized the cell; deflection the other way hyperpolarized it.
cards.section: At rest, then pushed both ways

cards.front: Inner hair cells sit with few transduction channels open at rest. A symmetric high-frequency tone vibrates the bundle back and forth. Predict the average receptor potential and why it matters for transmitter release.
cards.back: A steady depolarization for as long as the sound lasts. On the lower, curved part of the S-shaped opening curve, one half-cycle opens more channels than the other closes, so mean inward current rises. The membrane time constant filters out most of the cycle-by-cycle swing at high frequencies, but the steady part survives and keeps release going.
cards.quote: a symmetric back-and-forth vibration opens more channels on one half-cycle than it closes on the other

cards.front: What are perilymph's K+ and Na+ contents, and how does endolymph's K+ content compare with the cell's cytoplasm?
cards.back: Perilymph is like ordinary extracellular fluid: low K+, high Na+. Endolymph is rich in K+, about as rich as the cell's own cytoplasm.
cards.quote: Its base and sides face perilymph, which is like ordinary extracellular fluid: low in K+ and high in Na+.
cards.section: What carries the current: one cell, two fluids

cards.front: Cochlear endolymph is held roughly +80 mV positive to perilymph in mammals; this voltage is the {{c1::endocochlear potential}}.
cards.quote: in the cochlea it is held positive to perilymph, by roughly +80 mV in mammals
cards.section: What carries the current: one cell, two fluids

cards.front: A cochlear hair cell's inside is at −50 mV and the endolymph at +80 mV, both measured against perilymph. K+ is about equally concentrated on the two sides of the top membrane. Find the driving force on K+ across the top membrane (outward positive) and the direction K+ moves.
cards.back: V across the top = −50 − (+80) = −130 mV. E_K ≈ 0 mV, so driving force = V − E ≈ −130 mV. Negative, so K+ is pushed in and the cell depolarizes.
cards.why: This is why K+ entry depolarizes a cochlear hair cell, the reverse of most neurons, where K+ leaves.
cards.quote: The driving force is about −130 mV: negative, so K+ is pushed in, hard.
cards.section: What carries the current: one cell, two fluids

cards.front: Across a cochlear hair cell's basal membrane, the inside is at −50 mV and faces perilymph, where E_K is about −90 mV. Find the driving force on K+ (outward positive) and the direction K+ moves.
cards.back: −50 − (−90) = +40 mV. Positive, so K+ leaves the cell through potassium channels in the basal membrane.
cards.quote: The driving force is about +40 mV: positive, so K+ leaves, through potassium channels in the basal membrane.
cards.section: What carries the current: one cell, two fluids

cards.front: Why does a cochlear hair cell not need to pump out the K+ that enters through its transduction channels?
cards.back: K+ runs downhill the whole way: in at the top, driven by the +80 mV endolymph, and out at the base into low-K+ perilymph. The cochlea's wall recycles it; the battery is in the wall, not the cell.
cards.quote: So K+ runs downhill the whole way, in at the top and out at the bottom
cards.section: What carries the current: one cell, two fluids

cards.front: At steady state, a cochlear hair cell's K+ inflow at the top (driving force about 130 mV) equals its K+ outflow at the base (driving force about 40 mV). Roughly how does the basal open conductance compare with the top's?
cards.back: I = g × (V − E), so g_base × 40 = g_top × 130, giving g_base ≈ 3.25 × g_top: about three times the top's open conductance.
cards.quote: the base needs about three times the top's open conductance to pass the same current with about a third of the push
cards.section: What carries the current: one cell, two fluids

cards.front: A drug abolishes the endocochlear potential but leaves the hair cells unharmed; the cell's inside stays near −50 mV. Predict the current a given bundle push produces, and the effect on hearing.
cards.back: The current shrinks to well under half, and hearing becomes much less sensitive. With endolymph at 0 mV instead of +80 mV, the driving force across the top falls from about 130 mV to about 50 mV.
cards.quote: the driving force across the top membrane would fall from about 130 mV to about 50 mV
cards.section: What carries the current: one cell, two fluids

cards.front: Vestibular endolymph is only slightly positive. How does K+ entry into vestibular hair cells compare with cochlear hair cells, and why does K+ still enter?
cards.back: Vestibular hair cells run on a smaller driving force. K+ is still driven in at the top because the cell's inside is negative.
cards.quote: Vestibular endolymph is only slightly positive, so vestibular hair cells run on a smaller driving force than cochlear ones.

cards.front: How does a mature cochlear hair cell turn its receptor potential into a signal on its afferent fibre?
cards.back: Depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels at the base, and Ca2+ entry drives transmitter release. It fires no action potentials: a graded voltage sets a graded release rate.
cards.quote: In the mature cochlea the hair cell does not fire action potentials: a graded voltage sets a graded rate of release.

cards.front: A hair cell releases transmitter onto its afferent fibre at a {{c1::ribbon synapse}}, built for steady, graded release.
cards.quote: The release site is a ribbon synapse, built for steady, graded release

cards.front: Inner hair cells from mice lacking the L-type Ca2+ channel CaV1.3 are depolarized. What happens to exocytosis, and what does the result show?
cards.back: Exocytosis is only marginal. The result shows CaV1.3 is the voltage-gated Ca2+ channel whose opening drives transmitter release in these cells.
cards.quote: Mouse inner hair cells lacking the L-type channel CaV1.3 showed only marginal depolarization-evoked exocytosis

cards.front: Why does each place along the basilar membrane have its own natural frequency, and which end is tuned to high frequencies?
cards.back: The membrane is narrow and stiff near the base and wider and floppier toward the apex. Natural frequency is high where it is stiff, so the base is tuned high and the apex low.
cards.quote: Near the base, where sound enters, the membrane is narrow and stiff; toward the apex it is wider and more compliant, or floppy.
cards.section: The cochlea as a frequency map, and its amplifier

cards.front: Describe what a pure tone's travelling wave does as it moves along the basilar membrane.
cards.back: It moves from base to apex, slows and grows as it nears the place whose natural frequency matches the tone, peaks there, and dies away just beyond it.
cards.quote: A tone's wave slows and grows as it nears the place whose natural frequency matches it, peaks there
cards.section: The cochlea as a frequency map, and its amplifier

cards.front: The cochlea's mapping of frequency onto position, kept as a coarse gradient up to primary auditory cortex, is called {{c1::tonotopy}}.
cards.quote: This map is tonotopy, and it is kept, at least as a coarse gradient, through the main relays up to primary auditory cortex.
cards.section: The cochlea as a frequency map, and its amplifier

cards.front: What is the main code the brain uses to read pitch from the cochlea, and what supplements it at low frequencies?
cards.back: Mainly place: where along the basilar membrane the active hair cells are. At low frequencies the timing of nerve-fibre spikes also carries pitch.
cards.quote: That is the main code for pitch, but at low frequencies the timing of spikes also carries it.
cards.section: The cochlea as a frequency map, and its amplifier

cards.front: A human cochlea is modelled by Greenwood's function, f = 165.4 × (10^(2.1x) − 0.88), with f in Hz and x the fraction of length measured from the apex. In a 35 mm cochlea, how far from the base does a 2,000 Hz tone peak?
cards.why: x counts from the apex, so subtract from the full length to get distance from the base.
cards.quote: Step 1: rearrange. x = log10(f / 165.4 + 0.88) / 2.1.

cards.front: In a 35 mm human cochlea, 4,000 Hz peaks about 11.7 mm from the base. Using the rule that above about 1 kHz each octave takes about 5 mm, estimate where 8,000 Hz peaks.
cards.back: One octave higher, about 5 mm nearer the base: roughly 11.7 − 5 ≈ 6.7 mm from the base. (Greenwood's function gives about 6.8 mm.)
cards.quote: Above about 1 kHz, each doubling of frequency takes nearly the same length of membrane, about 5 mm.

cards.front: How many rows of inner and outer hair cells are there, and which supplies most of the auditory nerve's afferent fibres?
cards.back: One row of inner hair cells, which supplies most afferents. Three rows of outer hair cells, which receive few afferents.
cards.quote: One row of inner hair cells supplies most of the auditory nerve's afferent fibres.

cards.front: Outer hair cells change length when their voltage changes; the motor is the membrane protein {{c1::prestin}}.
cards.back: Electromotility, driven by voltage, not by ATP.
cards.quote: The motor is the membrane protein prestin, driven by voltage, not by ATP.

cards.front: How do outer hair cells amplify basilar-membrane motion?
cards.back: The bundle is pushed and the voltage swings; prestin shortens and lengthens the cell, which is braced against the membrane. The push is timed with the membrane's motion, like pushing a swing, adding energy near the peak each cycle.
cards.why: The added energy sharpens tuning and raises sensitivity, most for quiet sounds.
cards.quote: The cell's push is timed to go with the membrane's motion, like pushing a swing in the direction it is already moving

cards.front: Outer hair cells are lost, but inner hair cells and their nerve fibres keep working. Predict the effects on quiet sounds, loud sounds and frequency tuning.
cards.back: Thresholds rise by tens of decibels, so sounds below the new threshold are no longer heard; tuning blurs; sounds loud enough to exceed the new threshold are still heard.
cards.why: Quiet sounds relied most on the outer-hair-cell boost, which also sharpened the peak; inner hair cells still report, and loud sounds were boosted little.
cards.quote: Hearing thresholds rise by tens of decibels, because quiet sounds relied most on the boost

cards.front: Prestin-knockout mice lose sensitivity and sharp cochlear tuning, but their outer hair cells are also less stiff. Design an experiment to test whether prestin's motor action, not just prestin, is needed for amplification, and name key controls.
cards.back: Knock in a mutant prestin that leaves little electromotility near the resting voltage, confirm outer-hair-cell mechanics and transduction are preserved, then test amplification. Such mice still lost amplification. Controls: transduction currents, surviving hair-cell counts at the ages tested, thresholds across frequencies.
cards.why: Deleting a protein removes everything it does, so a knockout cannot isolate one function.
cards.quote: So the knockout shows prestin is needed, not that its motor action is.

cards.front: Give the ascending auditory pathway from the auditory nerve to cortex.
cards.back: Cochlear nucleus (same side) → superior olivary complex (both sides; first major comparison of the two ears) → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate nucleus → auditory cortex.
cards.quote: Fibres ascend to the inferior colliculus, which supplies most of the input to the medial geniculate nucleus, which relays to auditory cortex

cards.front: A patient has a lesion confined to the right inferior colliculus. Would you expect deafness in one ear? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. Every level above the cochlear nucleus receives input from both ears, so each ear is still represented. Deafness in one ear points to the ear, auditory nerve or cochlear nucleus.
cards.quote: Because every level above the cochlear nucleus receives both ears, deafness in one ear points to the ear, the auditory nerve or the cochlear nucleus

cards.front: Define interaural time difference (ITD) and interaural level difference (ILD).
cards.back: ITD: the difference in a sound's arrival time between the ears. ILD: the difference in sound level between the ears, made because the head casts a sound shadow.
cards.quote: An interaural time difference (ITD) is the difference in arrival time between the ears.

cards.front: Treat the ears as two points 0.20 m apart, with sound speed 343 m/s. A distant source sits 45 degrees from straight ahead. Estimate the interaural time difference.
cards.back: ITD = d × sin(theta) / c = 0.20 m × 0.707 / 343 m/s ≈ 0.000412 s, about 412 microseconds.
cards.why: The point-ear model ignores the path around the head, so the value is right in scale only.
cards.quote: The extra path to the far ear is d × sin(theta), so ITD = d × sin(theta) / c

cards.front: How do medial superior olive (MSO) neurons encode interaural time differences, and at what frequencies mainly?
cards.back: They are excited by both cochlear nuclei and fire most when the two inputs arrive together: coincidence detectors. Mainly at low frequencies, where nerve spikes lock to the wave's phase.
cards.quote: Neurons in the medial superior olive (MSO) are excited by both cochlear nuclei and fire most when the two inputs arrive together: they are coincidence detectors.

cards.front: In Jeffress's delay-line model of sound localization, a sound comes from the left. Which coincidence detector fires most?
cards.back: The one whose left-ear input travels the longer path, by just enough to cancel the left ear's head start, so both inputs arrive together.
cards.why: Bird circuits are often cited as fitting this scheme; how mammals compute ITDs is still debated.
cards.quote: the detector that fires most is the one whose left-ear input travels the longer path, by just enough to cancel the head start

cards.front: A high-frequency sound is louder at the left ear than at the right. Which lateral superior olive (LSO) fires more, and what wiring makes it do so?
cards.back: The left LSO. Each LSO is excited by the ear on its own side and inhibited by the other ear through a relay in the trapezoid body, so its rate reports which ear is louder.
cards.quote: the left LSO fires more when the sound is louder on the left

cards.front: Why are interaural time differences used mainly at low frequencies and level differences mainly at high frequencies?
cards.back: At low frequencies nerve spikes lock to the wave's phase, so timing is available. At high frequencies the head shadow is large, so level differences are big. It is a tendency, not a wall.
cards.quote: Time at low frequencies and level at high frequencies is a tendency, not a wall.

cards.front: Neither ITDs nor ILDs tell above from below. What cue does, and what happened when adults' pinnae were reshaped with moulds?
cards.back: Spectral cues: the pinna's folds filter sound differently by elevation, and the brain learns them. With moulds, elevation judgments were poor at first, then progressively recovered with the moulds in place.
cards.quote: The folds of the pinna filter sound differently by elevation, changing its mix of frequencies, and the brain learns those spectral cues

cards.front: Hair cells are lost only near the base of both cochleas. Predict which tones become hard to hear and which sound-localization cue suffers most.
cards.back: High-frequency tones, because the base is tuned high. Interaural level differences suffer most, since they are used mainly at high frequencies; low-frequency time differences are largely spared.
cards.why: Rests on tonotopy (base high) and on LSO level coding working mainly at high frequencies, where the head shadow is large.
cards.quote: They handle ILDs, mainly at high frequencies, where the head shadow is large.

cards.front: In each semicircular canal, the ampulla holds the hair bundles in a gelatinous flap called the {{c1::cupula}}.
cards.quote: Each semicircular canal is a fluid-filled ring whose swelling, the ampulla, holds hair bundles in a gelatinous flap, the cupula.

cards.front: How does a semicircular canal detect head rotation?
cards.back: When the head rotates, endolymph lags by inertia, bends the cupula and deflects the hair bundles in it.
cards.quote: When the head rotates, endolymph lags by inertia, bends the cupula and deflects the bundles, so canals report rotation.

cards.front: A person is rotated in a chair at a steady speed for a long time. What happens to the canal afferent signal, and what do canal afferents signal during ordinary, changing head movements?
cards.back: The signal fades during the long steady turn. During ordinary movements canal afferents signal roughly head velocity, because drag in the narrow canal makes the cupula's bend track velocity rather than acceleration.
cards.quote: In a long turn at steady speed the signal fades.

cards.front: How do paired semicircular canals on opposite sides encode a head turn, and what makes this push-pull possible?
cards.back: A turn excites one partner and inhibits the other. It works because each side's afferents fire at rest, so one side's rate can rise while the other's falls.
cards.quote: Canals on opposite sides pair in one plane, and a turn excites one partner while inhibiting the other.

cards.front: Suppose hair cells had no transduction channels open at rest and canal afferents were silent at rest. Predict which bundle deflections could be signalled and how a canal pair would report a head turn.
cards.back: Only deflection toward the tallest stereocilia; the other way could not reduce current below zero. A canal pair would lose push-pull: only the excited side would signal, since the inhibited side could not lower its rate.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that two-way signalling needs a resting current or resting firing to go up from and down from.
cards.quote: This push-pull works because each side's afferents already fire at rest, just as some transduction channels are open at rest

cards.front: The head turns quickly to the right. Trace the horizontal vestibulo-ocular reflex from canal to eye muscles.
cards.back: Right horizontal canal excited, left inhibited. Right vestibular nucleus excites the left abducens nucleus, driving the left lateral rectus; abducens interneurons cross via the MLF to the right oculomotor nucleus, driving the right medial rectus. Both eyes move left.
cards.why: Mirror image of the leftward-turn circuit.
cards.quote: The left vestibular nucleus excites the right abducens nucleus, whose motor neurons drive the right lateral rectus and turn the right eye rightward.

cards.front: During a head turn at 50 degrees per second, the eyes counter-rotate at 45 degrees per second. What is the vestibulo-ocular reflex gain, and how fast does the image slip across the retina?
cards.back: Gain = eye speed / head speed = 45 / 50 = 0.90. Retinal slip = 50 − 45 = 5 degrees per second.
cards.why: The cerebellum corrects a wrong gain.
cards.quote: The reflex's gain is eye speed divided by head speed, with the eyes turning the opposite way.

cards.front: A lesion interrupts the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) fibres that carry abducens-interneuron signals to the left oculomotor nucleus. The head turns quickly to the left. Predict each eye's reflex movement.
cards.back: The right eye still turns right, since the right abducens nucleus drives the right lateral rectus directly. The left eye fails to turn right, because the left medial rectus loses its drive. The eyes become misaligned.
cards.why: Rests on the circuit: right abducens motor neurons move the right eye; its interneurons reach the left oculomotor nucleus only through the MLF.
cards.quote: Abducens interneurons cross and run up the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to the left oculomotor nucleus

cards.front: The left labyrinth (the vestibular organs of the left inner ear) is suddenly destroyed while the head is still. What does the brain conclude, and what do the eyes do?
cards.back: It concludes the head is turning right. The eyes drift slowly left with quick jerks back to the right (nystagmus), and the room seems to spin (vertigo).
cards.why: The right side's resting firing is no longer matched by the left, the pattern a rightward turn produces.
cards.quote: the healthy right side's resting firing is no longer matched by the left, and that is the pattern a rightward turn produces

cards.front: What do the otolith organs (utricle and saccule) sense, and what caps their hair bundles?
cards.back: Linear (straight-line) acceleration and gravity. The bundles are capped by a membrane loaded with calcium carbonate crystals.
cards.quote: The otolith organs sense linear (straight-line) acceleration and gravity.

cards.front: Why can a passenger in an accelerating aircraft, with no view outside, feel tipped back?
cards.back: Forward acceleration shears the otolith membrane backward, the same shear a backward tilt gives, so otolith afferents alone cannot tell tilt from linear acceleration.
cards.quote: it shears the otolith membrane backward, as a backward tilt would

cards.front: Otolith signals alone cannot separate a head tilt from a linear translation. Which other vestibular signal could, and what should happen to eye responses to translation if that signal is removed?
cards.back: Semicircular canal signals: a tilt rotates the head, which the canals feel, while a translation does not. Without canal input, eye responses to translation should follow the ambiguous otolith signal, as found in rhesus monkeys after canal inactivation.
cards.quote: A tilt rotates the head, which the canals feel; a straight-line acceleration does not.

cards.front: The same hair-cell switch serves the cochlea, the semicircular canals and the otolith organs. For each, what pushes the bundle and what does the brain read?
cards.back: Cochlea: a travelling wave peaking at one place per frequency; the brain reads pitch from place. Canals: endolymph lagging during rotation bends the cupula; head rotation, roughly head velocity during ordinary, changing movements, and the signal fades during a long turn at steady speed. Otoliths: a crystal-loaded membrane shearing; tilt or translation, told apart with canal help.
cards.quote: One switch. A wave, a ring of fluid, a heavy membrane.
